lesson.title: What a Statistic Actually Tells You
lesson.summary: A statistic is a number calculated from sample data that estimates an unknown fact about a population, and this distinction between statistic and parameter is the foundation of all inferential reasoning in statistics.
lesson.body:
In statistics, the word population refers to the entire group you actually care about, and a parameter is a fixed number that describes that population, such as the true mean height of every sophomore at a school or the true proportion of all voters who support a candidate. The trouble is that parameters are almost always unknown, because measuring an entire population is expensive, slow, or simply impossible. A statistic solves this practical problem: it is a number calculated from a sample, a smaller subset of the population, and it is used as an estimate of the corresponding parameter. The sample mean, sample proportion, and sample standard deviation are all statistics, while the population mean, population proportion, and population standard deviation are the parameters they are trying to estimate.

This distinction only works if the sample was collected well. A statistic built from a sample is a meaningful estimate of a population parameter only when the sample reasonably represents the population, which is why random sampling matters so much. A convenience sample, such as surveying only your friends about their favorite subject, produces a statistic that may be far from the true parameter because the sample itself is biased. Good statistical practice starts with a well chosen sample and only then moves to computing a statistic from it.

Consider a concrete example. Suppose a school wants to know the mean height of all 400 sophomores, a population parameter usually written with the Greek letter mu. Measuring all 400 students is impractical, so instead five students are chosen at random and their heights in inches are recorded: 64, 68, 70, 66, and 72. The sample mean is found by adding these values and dividing by the sample size: 64 plus 68 plus 70 plus 66 plus 72 equals 340, and 340 divided by 5 equals 68. That value, 68 inches, is a statistic, commonly written as x with a bar over it, or x bar. It is our best single estimate of the unknown population mean mu, but it is not guaranteed to equal mu exactly.

Statistics are also used for categorical questions. Suppose 3 of those same 5 sampled students say they plan to attend an in state college. The sample proportion, written p hat, is 3 divided by 5, which equals 0.6, or 60 percent. This is an estimate of the true population proportion p, the fraction of all 400 sophomores who plan to attend in state.

One crucial fact about statistics is that they vary from sample to sample. If a different group of five students had been chosen at random, the sample mean height would almost certainly not be exactly 68 again, and the sample proportion would likely not be exactly 0.6 again. This natural fluctuation, called sampling variability, is not a mistake or a flaw in the method. It is an unavoidable feature of using a subset of data to estimate a whole, and it explains why later work in statistics focuses on describing how much a statistic tends to bounce around across different possible samples, rather than treating any single statistic as a perfect answer.
